Maladaptive Strategies.value: repeatedly blame myself for what happened
News reports about events similar to what happened to me

Threat.value: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds
I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me
I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building

Memory.value: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop
I can't seem to put the frightening event into words.
When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once

issues.item: Triggers: Offender Cues: Seeing the offender
issues.explanation: For terrorism trauma in a 70-year-old civilian dentist, 'seeing the offender' is hard to reconcile unless the patient had direct repeated exposure to an identified perpetrator; with the rest of the profile focused on generalized danger cues (uniforms, military topics, loud sounds, exits, watching others), this item stands out as clinically implausible for the same trauma context.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Evaluation: Situations in which other people evaluate me / my appearance / my performance
issues.explanation: 'Avoid evaluation' reflects social/performance-evaluation avoidance, but no threat, trigger, or memory items involve shame, scrutiny, appearance, or performance. It does not fit the otherwise terrorism-focused hypervigilance/trauma-reminder pattern and looks like a strategy for a different symptom cluster.

vignette:
Ernesto Villanueva is a 70-year-old widowed dentist of Colombian origin who has practiced in the same Miami clinic for nearly three decades. He came to the United States as a young man, built a quiet, ordered life, and prided himself on a steadiness that his patients and colleagues had always remarked upon. That steadiness was fractured approximately fourteen months ago when Ernesto was present at a civic ceremony in a public park - a local festival he attended every year - when a politically motivated attack unfolded without warning. Armed men in paramilitary-style clothing moved through the crowd, firing weapons and shouting directives. Ernesto was pinned behind a vendor's cart for what felt to him like an eternity, pressed against the ground, listening to shots ring out at irregular intervals, watching uniformed figures move past him with weapons raised. He was not physically wounded, but a man standing near him was struck and fell. Ernesto did not run. He stayed still, and he has never fully made peace with that fact.

In the weeks after the attack, Ernesto returned to his practice because he did not know what else to do. The clinic's routine - the hum of the suction unit, the bright overhead lights, the predictable sequencing of appointments - offered something that resembled normalcy. But the world outside the operatory had become a different place. When a car backfired on the street near his clinic, Ernesto found himself gripping the edge of the sink, unable to move for several seconds, the park flooding back through him not as a recollection but as a full sensory return: the smell of the grass, the weight of the ground beneath him, the sound of the shots as immediate and present as if they were occurring in the room. When the memory came in those moments, it did not arrive as narrative - he could not have told anyone, in ordered sentences, what had happened or in what sequence. It came as sensation, as texture, as the particular quality of light that afternoon, and it overwhelmed him so completely that he sometimes had to excuse himself from a patient mid-procedure and stand in the back hallway until the wave passed.

Ernesto had come to believe, with a certainty that felt irrefutable to him, that he should have done something more - pulled the man beside him to safety, acted rather than frozen. He returned to this conclusion repeatedly, rehearsing the moment from every angle, always arriving at the same verdict against himself. He began avoiding the evening news, because any report touching on political violence or armed groups confirmed, in his mind, that the world remained exactly as dangerous as it had been that afternoon. He started carrying a licensed firearm, which he kept in his car and sometimes in the inner pocket of his jacket, because what frightened him most was the idea of being caught without any means of response again.

At the clinic, the consequences of these changes became visible in ways Ernesto could not fully conceal. When a patient arrived wearing a security guard's uniform for an afternoon appointment, Ernesto felt his chest tighten and his attention fracture entirely. He got through the appointment by watching the man's hands. He now scans the waiting room each morning before unlocking the front door - not consciously cataloguing exits, but moving his eyes to every corner and doorway in a sweep that has become as automatic as washing his hands. He monitors his patients and his staff with a vigilance that has no clinical purpose, reading faces for signs of something he cannot name precisely but recognises immediately as threat.

A colleague gently noted that Ernesto seemed changed, and that several patients had mentioned he seemed distracted. A conversation about a recent news story involving military operations in South America left Ernesto unable to concentrate for the remainder of the afternoon. It was his daughter, calling from Bogotá, who finally said what had been unsaid - that her father did not sound like himself, and had not for over a year. Ernesto made the appointment the following week. What he most hopes for is to be able to remember what happened without being destroyed by it each time. What he fears most is that the man he was before the park no longer exists.
